stat_summary: In 2023/24, 73% of women in England had given money to charity in the previous four weeks, compared with 62% of men, according to the Community Life Survey. The overall figure was 67%. Buying goods from a charity shop or catalogue (28%) and giving by direct debit (23%) were the most common methods.
stat_source_title: Community Life Survey 2023/24: Volunteering and charitable giving, Department for Culture, Media and Sport

male.headline: The Quiet Fiver: 62 Per Cent of Men Gave to Charity Last Month, and Nobody Mentioned It
male.standfirst: New official figures confirm what every bloke already knows from the awkward shuffle at a collection tin: most British men still give, and they get precisely zero fuss about it, which is just how they like it, until they start to wonder.
male.image_caption: Malcolm, 61, slipping in a note. No sticker required.
body_paragraphs: New official figures have confirmed what every bloke already knows from the awkward shuffle at a collection tin: most British men still give. Sixty-two per cent had donated in the previous four weeks, and they received, in return, precisely zero fuss, which would be fine if anybody had at least nodded.

“I bought a book of raffle tickets at the rugby club and I've not heard a word since,” said Malcolm, 61, from Exeter. “For all I know I've funded a new roof. Nobody even offered me a warm sausage roll.”

The same survey finds buying from a charity shop and giving by direct debit are the most common methods, which campaigners say rather buries the quiet male donor who still stops at a tin and walks off without a sticker. They are already calling for a National Quiet Donor Day, and for a small nod – just a nod – for any man who has, in their words, “put a fiver in and kept walking”.
Yet where is the outrage? Where is the documentary? Britain's silent contributor pockets his change, alone, with only a lighter wallet for company.
male.pull_quote: For all I know I've funded a new roof. Nobody even offered me a warm sausage roll.

female.headline: Always Good for a Donation: 73 Per Cent of Women Gave Last Month, and They're Exhausted of Being Asked First
female.standfirst: Official statistics have finally measured the charitable load still landing on British women, and it does not look anything like a spontaneous fiver.
female.image_caption: Susan, 52, with the bag that has been in the hall since Tuesday.
body_paragraphs: Official statistics have at last measured the charitable load still landing on British women. Seventy-three per cent had given money in the previous four weeks – 11 points more than men – which, as any woman with a direct debit and a bag of clothes in the hall already knew, is not a coincidence.

“He puts a pound in a tin once a year and talks about it until Easter,” said Susan, 52, from Norwich. “I have three direct debits, a raffle book and a bag of clothes by the door, and nobody's made me chair of anything.”

Researchers note that buying from a charity shop is the most common method of giving, at 28 per cent, followed by direct debit at 23 per cent – both of which tend to involve someone remembering, bagging, and standing in a small queue. Campaigners are demanding a First-to-Be-Asked Act and a national apology for the phrase “you're better at this sort of thing”.
Until then, the country's unofficial fundraising department will keep a bag in the hallway, one outgrown coat at a time.
female.pull_quote: I have three direct debits, a raffle book and a bag of clothes by the door, and nobody's made me chair of anything.
